newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Zaire govt says Rwandan troops in east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Zaire govt says Rwandan troops in east Zaire.

text.p: Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo said in Belgium on Thursday that Rwandan troups have entered eastern Zaire to help Tutsi rebels there.

"Rwandan troops are in Zaire, in the north and the south of the Kivu province. We cannot accept this situation," Kengo told a news conference after a meeting with Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene.
The Rwandan government denies its forces have crossed into Zaire to fight alongside the Banyamulenge rebels.
"Rwanda must withdraw from Zaire. Zaire will defend its rights with all means at its disposition," Kengo said.
Kengo refused to say how many Rwandan troops were on Zairean territory and declined to comment on the military situation. Heavy fighting was reported to be continuing in eastern Zaire.
He accused Rwanda's Tutsi regime of training guerilla forces of the Banyamulenge, a Zairean-based ethnic Tutsi group.

"We have material proof of the presence of Rwandan troops on our territory, and of the way in which these troops are training some of our compatriots, the Banyamulenge...and with them want to destabilise Zaire," Kengo said.
He gave no indications about the health of Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko, who is being treated cancer of the prostate in Switserland.
Kengo said that if the Banyamulenge had problems with their status in Zaire, these problems should be sorted out with the Zairean government, and not with the Rwandan government.
The Banyamulenge are denied Zairean nationality despite having arrived in the area up to 200 years ago.
In the past weeks there have been reports that the Zairean army has driven the Banyamulenge from their homes in the towns of Bukavu and Uvira.
Kengo said he wanted to start talks with the Rwandan regime about the conflict and called on Belgium -- former colonial ruler of both Zaire and Rwanda -- to play a mediating role.
He also warned that the fighting was threathening the food supply of the camps of Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire.
Kengo is on a lightning visit to Europe to discuss the explosive situation in Central Africa's Great Lakes region.
Earlier on Thursday he also met with the European Union's special envoy for the Great Lakes region, Aldo Ajello.
EU sources told Reuters that Ajello had expressed the EU's willingness to defuse tension in the area and to relieve the plight of the refugees.
Diplomats and aid officials have said they fear Tutsi-dominated armies in Burundi and Rwanda could be drawn into the fighting, sparking wider conflict.
